title: Air India 855
summary: Air India Flight 855 crashed into the Arabian Sea approximately one minute after takeoff from Mumbai on January 1, 1978, killing all 213 people aboard. The Boeing 747-237B, registered VT-EBD, experienced a loss of control during the right turn over the Arabian Sea. The captain's attitude direction indicator (ADI) had toppled but he misinterpreted the first officer's statement about his own toppled ADI, believing both indicated a right bank. Over the dark Arabian Sea with no external visual references, the captain made control inputs to increase the left bank, causing the aircraft to roll beyond recovery and crash into the sea.
probable_cause: Irrational control inputs by the captain following complete unawareness of the aircraft's attitude due to a malfunctioned ADI, with the crew failing to gain control using other flight instruments.

factors.evidence: Captain Kukar was explaining that his attitude direction indicator (ADI) had toppled, meaning that it was still showing the aircraft in a right bank
First Officer Virmani, whose presumably functional ADI was now showing a left bank and not noticing the captain's concern, said Mine has also toppled
It was after sunset and the aircraft was flying over a dark Arabian Sea, leaving the aircrew unable to visually cross-check their ADI instrument readings with the actual horizon

the jet hit the Arabian Sea at an estimated 35-degree nose-down angle, having rolled to 108 degrees

title: Pacific Western Airlines 314
summary: Pacific Western Airlines Flight 314, a Boeing 737, crashed at Cranbrook Airport on February 11, 1978. The aircraft touched down about 800 feet from the runway threshold in snowing conditions with visibility of 3/4 mile. The pilots did not see a snowplow on the runway. To avoid collision, the captain immediately disengaged reverse thrust but one engine remained at idle reverse and the other at full forward thrust. The asymmetric thrust configuration rendered the aircraft uncontrollable. Calgary ATC had miscalculated the flight's arrival time. The aircraft crashed, killing 43 of 49 on board.
probable_cause: Asymmetric thrust reverser deployment after aborted landing to avoid snowplow, combined with ATC arrival time calculation error and crew failure to report beacon passage.

With flaps 25 and gear down, it was not possible to maintain level flight with asymmetric reverse thrust

summary: Two minutes after takeoff from Caracas, the crew declared an emergency and reported problems with the attitude indicator. The aircraft crashed into the sea with all occupants killed. Major aircraft wreckage recovery was not possible due to water depth.

title: 1978 Balkan Bulgarian Tupolev Tu-134 crash
summary: Balkan Bulgarian Airlines Flight 107 crashed near Gabare, Bulgaria, 10 minutes after takeoff from Sofia. The aircraft experienced abnormal turns and descent. A 2024 investigation found evidence that the aircraft was most likely hijacked in-flight and crashed as a result of onboard fighting, though the official 1978 investigation attributed the cause to an electrical malfunction.
probable_cause: The official investigation cited malfunction of electrical installation. However, a 2024 investigation by Biograph journal found witnesses who testified that the aircraft had two unlisted passengers who were most likely DS-trained agents from Arab countries, and the aircraft was most likely hijacked in-flight and crashed as a result of onboard fighting.

title: Air Rhodesia 825
summary: Vickers Viscount shot down by ZIPRA surface-to-air missile on starboard wing during Rhodesian Bush War. Aircraft forced to attempt emergency belly landing in cotton field west of Karoi. Impact with ditch caused aircraft to cartwheel and break up, killing 38 on impact. Surviving 10 found in wreckage then massacred by insurgents; 8 total survivors.
probable_cause: Hostile act by Zimbabwe People's Revolutionary Army with Soviet-made Strela-2 infrared missile.

title: Pacific Southwest Airlines 182
summary: PSA Flight 182, a Boeing 727, collided mid-air with a Cessna 172 during approach to San Diego on a clear day with 10 miles visibility. The PSA crew lost visual contact with the Cessna despite ATC instructions to maintain visual separation and did not report the loss of sight. The NTSB determined the probable cause was the PSA flight crew's failure to follow proper air traffic control procedures.
probable_cause: The probable cause of the accident was the failure of the PSA flight crew to follow proper air traffic control procedures. Flight 182's crew lost sight of the Cessna in contravention of ATC instructions to keep visual separation from that traffic and did not alert ATC that they had lost sight of it. Errors on the part of ATC were also named as contributing factors, including the use of visual separation procedures when radar clearances were available.

title: Aeroflot 1080
summary: Aeroflot Flight 1080 took off at 19:48 from Sverdlovsk at an overloaded weight in cloudy, rainy, 5°C conditions. At 19:50, just 100 meters off the ground, the left engine failed due to icing. All three engines were affected by ice accretion. With the left engine failed and the right and center engines producing insufficient power, the aircraft could not maintain altitude. It struck trees at 23 meters while still climbing and crashed, killing all 38 on board.
probable_cause: Icing conditions combined with aircraft overload and crew failure to account for icing effects on all engines, resulting in insufficient power to maintain altitude after left engine failure.

title: Icelandic Airlines 001
summary: Loftleiðir Flight 001 crashed on approach to Colombo on November 15, 1978. The crew was cleared to descend on runway 22 for an ILS approach. The approach controller warned the flight was undershooting but the crew was speaking with the radar controller on another frequency and did not receive the advisory. The aircraft descended dangerously towards the ground and crashed into a rubber and coconut plantation. The crash killed 183 out of 262 passengers and crew.
probable_cause: The official report determined the probable cause to be the failure of the crew to conform to approach procedures. During the approach, the crew did not properly monitor descent rate and position.

title: Alitalia 4128
summary: Alitalia Flight 4128 was a scheduled flight from Rome to Palermo with 129 persons on board. On 23 December 1978, the Douglas DC-9-32 crashed into the Tyrrhenian Sea about 3 km north of Palermo while on approach. The accident was attributed to the flight deck crew believing they were nearer to the runway than they were. The crew stopped descent at 150 ft above the sea, then flew level at 150 knots, thinking they were close to the runway because of airport lights. The aircraft lost altitude due to wind and impacted the water with its right wing, killing 108 of the 129 on board.
probable_cause: The accident was attributed to the flight deck crew believing they were nearer to the runway than they were, leading to premature descent and misjudgment of position during the final approach phase.

title: United Airlines 173
summary: Flight 173 ran out of fuel during a prolonged hold caused by a landing gear problem. While the crew troubleshot the gear with the landing gear down and flaps extended, fuel consumption was greatly increased but not adequately monitored. Due to cockpit culture, the first officer and flight engineer failed to assertively communicate the critical fuel situation to the captain. All four engines flamed out due to fuel starvation, and the aircraft crashed in a suburban Portland area with 10 fatalities. This accident prompted the development of crew resource management training.
probable_cause: The flight crew became so absorbed with diagnosing the landing gear problem that they failed to monitor their fuel state and calculate a time when they needed to return to land or risk fuel exhaustion.

factors.evidence: The right main landing gear retract cylinder assembly had failed due to corrosion, allowing the right gear to free fall and damage a microswitch that prevented the green light from illuminating.
